description_full: Zebra Technologies Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates in the automatic identification and data capture solutions industry worldwide. It operates in two segments, Connected Frontline, and Asset Visibility and Automation. The company designs, manufactures, and sells printers that produce labels, wristbands, tickets, receipts, and plastic cards; dye-sublimination thermal card printers that produce images, which are used for personal identification, access control, and financial transactions; radio frequency identification device (RFID) printers that encode data into passive RFID transponders; accessories and options for printers, including carrying cases, vehicle mounts, and battery chargers; stock and customized thermal labels, receipts, ribbons, plastic cards, and RFID tags for printers; and electronic sensors and temperature-monitoring labels. It also provides various maintenance, technical support, repair, and managed and professional services; fixed readers, RFID enabled mobile computers, and RFID sleds; tags, sensors, exciters, middleware software, and application software; and physical inventory management solutions; rugged and enterprise-grade mobile computing products and accessories, as well as real-time location systems and services. In addition, the company offers barcode scanners and imagers, RFID readers, industrial machine vision cameras, and fixed industrial scanners; point-of-sale solutions, self-serve kiosks, and interactive touchscreen displays; workflow optimization solutions, such as workforce management, workflow execution and task management, and prescriptive analytics, and communications and collaboration solutions; and cloud-based software. The company serves retail and e-commerce, manufacturing, transportation and logistics, healthcare, public sector, and other industries through direct sales force and network of channel partners. The company was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in Lincolnshire, Illinois.

financial_summary: Zebra Technologies Corporation is a large-cap technology business with a $15.2B market cap on $5.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 47%.

The business throws off $831M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.19× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.4×.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 13% operating margin runs 6pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.55x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-13.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 49% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 1.47, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $199.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2020 crash, 61% in the 2022 bear market and 57% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 18% below its DCF fair value of $394, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 27%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $256 to $607 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/FCF 18.2 vs 25.4 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-9%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $417 on average, 30% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 11% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It runs a 47% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow, or 12% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.19x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 11.0% of revenue on R&D and 3.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($125.0M of cash against $2.5B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.4x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.6, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.97 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 56% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.3% over 3 years, 3.9% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 32%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 16% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 11%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (3.9% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 10,700 employees, each generates about $504K of revenue, 1.4x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 12.2% a year.
That works out to $78K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
